an3.74:1.1: The lack of reference to the Buddha suggests this may have been after his passing.
an3.74:1.2: Abhaya also appears in [an4.196](), while Paṇḍitakumāra appears only here.
an3.74:1.3: The Jain leader Mahāvīra Vardhamāna is known as Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta in Pali texts. He is regarded as the 24th supreme leader of the Jains, although only he and his predecessor Pārśvanātha (not mentioned in the Pali) are historical. _Nigaṇṭha_ means “knotless” (i.e. without attachments); it is a term for a Jain ascetic. Nātaputta indicates his clan the Ñātikas (Sanskrit _jñātiputra_; Prākrit _nāyaputta_). The Pali tradition has confused _ñāti_ (“family”) with _nāṭa_ (“dancer”). Thus Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta means “the Jain monk of the Ñātika clan”.
an3.74:1.4: Such extraordinary claims were not unprecedented, as both Mahāvīra ([mn14:17.2](), [mn79:6.7]()) and Pūraṇa Kassapa ([an9.38:2.1]()) are said to claim omniscience in the Pali canon. Extant Jain texts have no shortage of such claims (eg. Sūyagaḍa1.6, Kalpasūtra 1, Bhagavatisūtra 4.10, etc.), and it seems this was a genuine teaching of Mahāvīra.
an3.74:1.5: Jains believed that karma was material, made up of particles. The practice of _tapas_ (“fervent mortification”) creates an intense bodily heat which burns off these karmic particles, freeing the soul (_jīva_) to shine in its intrinsic purity. | The idiom “breaking the bridge” is not otherwise found in parallels to this passage ([mn14:17.7]()). It is used a few times by the Buddha in the sense of making a final and complete break with something ([an3.107:1.4](), [an4.159:4.8](), [pli-tv-bu-vb-pj1:2.1.10]()).
an3.74:1.6: The future tense with past participle is a rare example of future perfect in Pali (see also [mn14:17.8](), [mn81:4.3]()). | This sentence is constructed similarly to Buddhist teachings, but the sequence of ideas is not really coherent. The mention of “feeling” after “suffering” here is found consistently in Pali sources, but not in their parallels.
an3.74:1.7: The construction of this sentence parallels the Pali _evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti_.
an3.74:2.4: The idiom _phussa phussa_ (literally, “having repeatedly contacted”), while linguistically straightforward, is tricky to interpret. It is easy to read it as implying that experiencing the results of that past kamma is essential to its elimination. But this is not the intention, as shown by the use of the same idiom in [dn1:3.71.12](). There, it occurs in a rewording of the arising of dependent origination, where the repeated contact is not part of ending suffering, but is the continual ongoing, grinding experience of the suffering of feelings for one still stuck in transmigration. The sense here, therefore, is that, having endured for a long time the continual onslaught of pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings experienced by contact through the senses, one is finally freed. Pali _phassa_ (“contact”, “touch”) is closely connected with the idea of “experiencing”, and in this context with “feeling” in dependent origination. I try to bring out the sense by rendering “having suffered contact again and again”.
an3.74:2.5: The Jains believed that through the practice of austerities one could “wear away” past bad deeds ([mn14:17.5]()) and future suffering ([mn14:17.8]()). The Buddha distinguishes the term from self-mortification and adapts it for Buddhist use, with “wearing away” applied to the defilements that produce suffering ([sn42.12:22.1]()). It is applied to the tenfold path at [an10.106]().
an3.74:5.4: The threat of losing one’s head is found at eg. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.24, or at 3.9.26 when it actually did fall off.
